title: Best Time to Visit Kurseong and Mirik, Month by Month
meta_description: When to visit Kurseong, Mirik, Sittong and Latpanchar: clear views Oct–Dec, first flush tea and hornbills Mar–May, oranges in winter, and monsoon risks.
summary: October to December is the best time for clear mountain views, with November the quietest month. March to May is best for first flush tea, rhododendrons and hornbills at Latpanchar. Oranges ripen in Sittong from November to January. July and August bring heavy rain and landslides, so most travellers avoid them.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: This land sits lower than Darjeeling, mostly between 1,200 and 2,200 m, so it is a few degrees warmer and rarely sees snow. That makes it a good choice for the cold months, when Darjeeling is near freezing at night and Kurseong is still pleasant by day. The two best seasons are the same as elsewhere in the hills: October to December, when the air is clear after the monsoon, and March to May, when the tea gardens are busy and the forests are in new leaf.

If we had to choose one month it would be November. Puja crowds have gone, mornings are reliably clear, the autumn flush is being made and oranges are colouring in Sittong. Our second choice is March, for first flush tea and quiet roads. Avoid July and August unless you want rain, mist and empty hotels.
Rainfall decides almost everything here. These slopes face the plains and catch the monsoon head on, so the wet months are very wet, and the dry months are reliably dry and bright.

paras: Temperatures are typical daytime ranges for Kurseong at about 1,480 m; Mirik is similar, Chimney and Dow Hill are 3–5 °C colder, and Sittong and Latpanchar are a little warmer. Ratings are ours, for a budget traveller who wants views, walks and village life.

sections.heading: October to December: views and oranges
paras: The monsoon usually ends in late September or early October, and the first dry mornings bring the clearest air of the year. From Ahaldara above Latpanchar, the high bends of Dow Hill and the tea ridges above Mirik, the Kanchenjunga massif shows on most mornings until about 9 am, after which haze and cloud rise from the valleys. October is also festival season: Durga Puja, then Dashain and Tihar, when Kurseong's lanes fill with lamps and families visit each other. It is the busiest month for Bengali travellers, so rooms in Mirik and near Kurseong station need booking weeks ahead.

November is quieter and colder at night, about 9 °C in Kurseong and close to freezing at Chimney. December is the clearest month and the peak of the orange harvest in Sittong and the warmer pockets around Mirik. The Directorate of Cinchona has organised an orange festival at Sittong in December in past years; dates are announced locally, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: January and February: cold, clear and cheap
paras: Winter here is milder than in Darjeeling. Days in Kurseong reach 12–14 °C in the sun, nights drop to about 5 °C, and Mirik's lake can have a skin of mist at dawn. Views remain good through January, the last oranges are picked, and hotel prices are at their lowest outside Christmas and New Year. On 23 January Kurseong marks Netaji Jayanti at the Giddapahar museum.

February warms up, but haze from the plains starts to creep in later in the month. The tea bushes are pruned back and factories are mostly quiet, so it is not the time for tea tours. It is a good time for walking, because the trails over Dow Hill and down to Makaibari are dry and the air is cool. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, falls in February or March and is marked at Bokar monastery above Mirik.

sections.heading: March to May: tea, birds and blossom
paras: First flush starts in March, when the bushes put out their first young leaves after winter. Plucking restarts at Makaibari, Castleton, Gopaldhara and the Mirik valley gardens, and factories run again. This is the season for tasting and buying the lightest, most prized teas of the year. Rhododendrons flower on the higher ridges in March and April, and the forests of Dow Hill fill with fresh green.

For birders, April and May are the months to be at Latpanchar, when hornbills are active in the old trees near the sanctuary edge. Afternoon thunderstorms begin in late April and build through May, so plan walks for the mornings. May is the summer holiday month for families from Kolkata and the plains; Mirik's lake is at its busiest and Kurseong's hotels fill at weekends. Second flush, the muscatel season, starts late in May and runs into June.

sections.heading: June to September: the monsoon
paras: The monsoon usually reaches these hills by mid-June. The first half of June is often pleasant, and second-flush tea is still being made. From late June to early September rain falls most days, often heavily, and landslides are common on the Hill Cart Road, the Rohini road and the roads to Sittong and Latpanchar. The lower section of the toy train has been suspended for long periods by slips at Pagla Jhora and Tindharia. Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuary closes to visitors in the monsoon, and leeches are out on every forest path.

There are reasons to come anyway. The gardens are at their greenest, hotels drop prices, and naturalists come to Namthing Pokhri, where Himalayan salamanders breed in July and August; keep to the edge and do not handle them. September is a good compromise as the rain eases and the autumn flush begins. Roads and the toy train change quickly in these months, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Crowds, holidays and booking ahead
paras: Weather is only half the choice. The other half is who else is travelling. Kurseong and Mirik are a short drive from Siliguri, so they fill on ordinary weekends as well as holidays, with families coming up for a night by the lake or a day on the toy train. Friday and Saturday nights cost more than weekday nights in most Mirik hotels, and the Sunday afternoon jeeps back to Siliguri are full by midday.

The four peak periods are Durga Puja and the week after it, Diwali, Christmas to New Year, and mid-May to mid-June, when schools in West Bengal and the plains are closed. In those weeks book rooms two to four weeks ahead, travel up early in the morning, and expect village homestays in Sittong to be booked by groups. Outside them, you can usually find a bed on arrival, though we still suggest booking the first night.

If your dates are fixed in a wet or crowded week, choose the villages over the towns. Chimney, Latpanchar and the Makaibari homestays stay quieter than Mirik's lake road even in October, and a homestay host will tell you honestly whether the road in is open.

sections.heading: Choosing by what you want
paras: Most travellers have one thing in mind. Use this list to match it to a month, then check the toy train and road status for your dates.

faqs.q: What is the best month to visit Kurseong?
faqs.a: November is our pick. Puja crowds have gone, mornings are reliably clear, the autumn flush is being made in the gardens and nights are cold but not freezing in town. October and December are almost as good. For tea lovers, March and April are better, because first flush is being plucked and the factories are working at full pace.

faqs.q: Does it snow in Kurseong or Mirik?
faqs.a: Snow is very rare. Kurseong and Mirik sit at about 1,480–1,500 m, well below the snowline, and winter nights fall to about 5 °C rather than below freezing. The higher ridges at Chimney and Dow Hill, around 1,900–2,200 m, are colder and very occasionally see frost or a light dusting. For snow, you need to go much higher, to Sandakphu or North Sikkim.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Kurseong and Mirik?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear mornings from mid-October to January, and sometimes in March. The best viewpoints are Ahaldara above Latpanchar, the high bends of the Dow Hill road and the ridges above Mirik on the Darjeeling road. Go early: by 9 or 10 am haze and cloud usually rise from the valleys. From June to September views are rare.

faqs.q: Is it safe to visit Kurseong in the monsoon?
faqs.a: It is possible but needs care. From late June to September, landslides close or slow the Hill Cart Road, the Rohini road and the roads to Sittong and Latpanchar, sometimes for days. Travel in daylight, keep spare days and cash, and avoid forest walks in heavy rain. Toy train services are often suspended, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the orange season in Sittong?
faqs.a: Darjeeling mandarins in Sittong ripen from about mid-November and are picked through December into January, with the peak in December. Orchard oranges cost about ₹60–120 a kg in season. The Directorate of Cinchona has organised an orange festival at Sittong in December in past years; dates are announced locally, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is first flush tea season in Kurseong?
faqs.a: First flush runs from about March to April, when the bushes put out new leaves after winter dormancy. Second flush follows from late May into June, and the autumn flush from October to November. Factory visits are most rewarding in these months. From December to February the bushes are pruned and most factories are quiet.

faqs.q: Is Mirik crowded during Durga Puja?
faqs.a: Yes. Durga Puja, which falls in late September or October, is Mirik's busiest season, with families from Kolkata and Siliguri filling lakeside hotels and boats. Prices can double and jeeps fill fast. Book rooms several weeks ahead, or come in the first half of November, when the weather is as good and the lake is much quieter.

faqs.q: What should I pack for Kurseong in winter?
faqs.a: From December to February, pack a warm jacket, a fleece or sweater, a woollen cap and warm socks, because nights in Kurseong fall to about 5 °C and are colder at Chimney or Dow Hill. Days are mild in the sun, so layers work best. Homestays provide quilts, but a light thermal set helps in houses without heaters.

faqs.q: When is the best time for birdwatching at Latpanchar?
faqs.a: March to May is the best period, when hornbills and other forest birds are active and calling in the old trees near the edge of Mahananda sanctuary. Go out at dawn with a local guide, who will know the current fruiting trees. October to February is also good for resident birds. The sanctuary closes in the monsoon, so check current status before you travel.
